content: If the respondent asks for more information, refer to the explanation below. Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) refers to starting ART in individuals with HIV when their CD4 count is above 500. In 2013, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended initiating ART when the CD4 count is ≤500, which was an update from the previous guidance of ≤350. Currently, WHO does not recommend starting ART for individuals with a CD4 count >500, except in specific cases. These exceptions include people with HIV and active tuberculosis (TB), those co-infected with HIV and hepatitis B with evidence of severe chronic liver disease, and individuals in serodiscordant relationships (where one partner is HIV-positive and the other is HIV-negative) to reduce transmission to the uninfected partner. In these cases, ART should be initiated regardless of CD4 count. Some countries are now recommending or considering recommending that all men who have sex with men (MSM) should start ART regardless of their CD4 count. Taking ART, regardless of CD4 count, can significantly reduce HIV transmission to others, either through sexual contact or shared equipment. WHO recommends that everyone with a CD4 count of 500 or below should be on ART for their health and to prevent transmission to others. It is not yet clear whether starting ART when the CD4 count is >500 provides direct health benefits to the individual, but it does have a preventive effect. This approach to early ART initiation is sometimes referred to as treatment as prevention (TasP). Some experts suggest that early ART (CD4 >500) should be recommended for all MSM to help prevent transmission to others. Understanding Check: Is this explanation helpful? Do you have any questions? How would you explain early initiation of ART? If HIV-positive: Are you currently on ART? If yes: When did you start? Did you start ART because of your health status, for prevention reasons, or for another reason (e.g., to start a family)? Please explain your answer. If it was for prevention: Did you face any particular challenges in starting ART for prevention reasons? If so, what were they? What benefits have you experienced from starting ART for prevention? If no: What is your view on early initiation of ART (CD4 500 or above) as a preventive intervention? Is this something you would consider if it were available in your area? If yes: Why would you consider this? What would help you make a decision about early ART? More information—what specific information would you find most helpful? Support from service providers? Access? What are your potential concerns or challenges about starting ART at a higher CD4 count (or before feeling sick)? For Experts and Service Providers: 1. What are your views on early initiation of ART? Are these views the same for adolescent and young MSM? Please explain. 2. What are the potential benefits of offering early initiation of ART to MSM? 3. What are your concerns about offering early initiation of ART to MSM? In relation to service provision? In relation to your clients? In relation to adolescent and young clients? 4. What strategies do you think could address these challenges? 5. What do you advise your MSM clients about early initiation of ART? Is your advice the same for adolescent and young clients? For Service Providers Only: 1. Have you ever prescribed early initiation of ART for MSM? If yes: Tell me about your experiences. What challenges did you face as a service provider? What challenges did your clients face? What strategies helped you or your clients address these challenges? If no: Why have you not offered early initiation of ART to MSM? Is it not available? Is it not appropriate? Please explain. Was it offered but the client refused? What were the main reasons for the client’s refusal? What would assist in improving the acceptability of early initiation of ART for MSM? Information? Access? Discrimination/Violence: If issues of discrimination or violence arose during the interview: Earlier, you mentioned discrimination or violence. I would like to ask you some further questions about that, if it is okay with you. If not previously discussed: I would like to ask you some questions about how MSM are treated in your country. How are MSM treated in your country? What are the attitudes of health providers toward MSM? How do health providers treat MSM? How have these attitudes and experiences affected MSM’s ability to access sexual health services? What experiences have you had with violence directed at you or other men because of being MSM? Legal Issues: What kinds of legal assistance do MSM need? Where do MSM go for legal assistance? How does the legal system respond to MSM? Closing: Thank you very much for your time. I appreciate your willingness to share your personal experiences, views, and feelings. Is there anything else you would like to add at this time? Reminder: Please be assured that I will not include any identifying information about you personally in the report. Feel free to contact MSMGF staff if you have any questions or would like to provide feedback. Would you like me to repeat their contact information for your convenience? Thank you again for your time today. Is this a good time to end the call?
